newsitem.title: ITALY: Italy's Bertinotti says govt talks "constructive".
newsitem.headline: Italy's Bertinotti says govt talks "constructive".

text.p: The leader of Italy's hard-left Communist Refoundation said on Thursday that talks with the main party in the centre-left coalition to try and resolve potentially destabilising differences had been useful.
"The climate is constructive," Refoundation leader Fausto Bertinotti said after a two and a half hour meeting with Democratic Party of the Left (PDS) head Massimo D'Alema.
PDS sources meanwhile said the meeting between the two "basically went well".

Bertinotti brushed aside questions about whether the survival of the centre-left government, which does not include Refoundation but depends on the hard-left party for its majority in the lower house of parliament, was in danger.
"One can say that the political intention is to make this coalition live in self-sufficient terms," he told reporters.
Armando Cossutta, Refoundation parliamentary leader, said that he believed "the conditions for an agreement are there.
"Naturally, differences remain but there is certainly not the sense of a showdown," he added.

Bertinotti has met leading government figures in recent days to try to resolve deep differences between his party and the ruling coalition over a planned supplementary budget, privatisations and reform of the welfare state.
Bertinotti said he and D'Alema discussed issues linked to the privatisation of state telecoms company Stet, electricity giant Enel as well as assessing the political climate.
"The meeting was useful," he said, adding that the time was ripe for a meeting of all the centre-left coalition forces to discuss pressing problems such as jobs.
PDS sources said D'Alema had assured Bertinotti that the government had no intention of realigning itself.

The centre-right Freedom Alliance of opposition leader Silvio Berlusconi has recently put out feelers to the government, offering its support "in the country's interest" to pass legislation opposed by Refoundation.
Prime Minister Romano Prodi has pledged to introduce a mini-budget in the coming weeks with up to 14.6 trillion lire ($8.5 billion) of deficit-cutting measures.

Bertinotti has already said he will not accept tax hikes or cuts in welfare spending, drastically limiting Prodi's options as he fights to contain the state deficit and book Italy a place on the launch of the single European currency.
The government and Refoundation are also negotiating over the planned sale later this year of telecom giant Stet, to which the hard-left is ideologically opposed.
The privatisation still needs parliamentary legislation and without a deal between Prodi and Bertinotti, the long delayed sell-off would be doomed to another postponment.

Corriere della Sera newspaper reported on Thursday that a meeting between Prodi and Bertinotti on Wednesday had been "icy". Financial daily Il Sole 24 Ore said the two sides were as far apart as ever.
The two men were due to meet again on Thursday.
